items.body:
Chicago quartet U.S. Maple's best album, 'Acre Thrills' is an American avant-rock masterpiecce that torches established formula unremittingly, singlehandedly creating music that's never quite been repeated - or bettered. Essential listening FFO Gastr del Sol, Hella, even black midi.

By the time U.S. Maple released 'Acre Thrills' in 2001, they'd already proved what they needed to prove, building up a so-called "math rock" sound out of the bones of Captain Beefheart's deconstructed 'Trout Mask Replica' and tearing it apart on the fly. And even when they brushed with the college rock underground's top levels, opening for Pavement and potentially glomming onto a completely new audience, they stuck to their guns, getting weirder rather than sanding down their sharp edges. This album isn't as dark as its predecessor by any means (we're gonna blame 'Talker' producer Michael Gira for that one), but it's more delicately arranged somehow - a perfectly imperfect lattice of angular, xenharmonic riffs and interlock'd polyrhythms that still somehow manage to couch vocalist Al Johnson's almost inhuman groans and monologues. His delivery's like Marmite, undoubtedly, but it's another element of the U.S. Maple sound that makes them impossible to properly replicate - despite bands endlessly trying ever since.

Although 'Acre Thrills' almost relishes its own knottiness, it's packed with moments that sound almost welcoming, at least to us. Opener 'Ma Digital' is surprisingly soft, Johnson's voice just a low hum underneath Mark Shippy and Todd Rittman's pretty breezy, almost hummable riffs, and if you didn't know better, you might confuse 'Babe' for a bluesier post-hardcore experiment, like Karate through a blender. By 'Untitled' though, their claws are fully on show with an instrumental that deconstructs itself as it plays through, falling apart into run-out-groove noise that's supposed to make you question what you're listening to. And when the album jolts back to life with 'Obey Your Concert', it's bolder, trickier and edgier, with Johnson veering from David Thomas to David Bowie in a matter of seconds. In the wrong hands, this kind of studied, hyper-technical grandstanding would be like nails on a chalkboard, so it's genuinely shocking that U.S. Maple managed to make it sound not just effortless but enduringly edgy. It's not noodly prog, it's grinding, painful, urgent music that understands the all-important polarity of blues, rock and all its variants.

Italian ambient maestro Gigi Masin returns to his happy place on 'Movement', following 2020's 'Calypso' with a record that surveys a quarter century of vintage back room sounds, pulling from kosmische, new age, early techno, glitch and balearic house. 

For the last few years, Masin has been busy with a litany of collaborations, working with Jonny Nash and Young Marco as Gaussian Curve, with dub techno OG Rod Modell on 2023's 'Red Hair Girl at Lighthouse Beach and with jazz pianist Greg Foat on a ruck of soundtrack-y downtempo material. In fact it's been years since his last solo release; the Apollo-released 'Calypso' came out six years ago and 'Movement' appears to pick up where it left off. The waterlogged, sun-bleached concept is all but gone, but the sounds, cherry-picked from across the downtempo spectrum, are very much in keeping. 

Opener 'Bed on Mars' is classic Masin and should appeal to fans of his cult 1986 breakout 'Wind', the long-overlooked album that featured 'Clouds', that new age/ambient anthem that relaunched his career after it was sampled by both To Rococo Rot and Björk. It's a fleeting moment, but it's packed to the brim with the good stuff: humid post-Vangelis pads, synthetic choirs and reflecting pools of reverb. And the atmosphere's pierced by loping rhythms almost immediately; 'Lost' matches its elasticated brass moans with a low-slung beat and then 'The Age of Sampling' appears to hark back to the Fairlight era, conjuring up an industrial soundscape with jerky low-bitrate drum hits, dialog samples and inclement textures that sound like they belong on Black Rain's 'Neuromancer' soundtrack.

The title track is even more surprising, a slippery 120bpm house groover that sounds as if it's been precision engineered for hazy sunrises, with sax wails and vocal pads ducking behind its rubbery beats. If that sounds a bit much, then there's a few quieter spells, like the piano-led 'UMI' and the Shuttle358-inspired closer 'Fifteen', but you can tell that for Masin, "ambient" doesn't mean beatless. The highlight, 'Deception Dance', sounds like classic beardy back-room techno, even - the sort of twitchy biz Carl Craig used to engineer when he was still moonlighting as 69.

items.body:
Thessa Torsing (aka upsammy) and drum deity Valentina Magaletti consolidate their intentions on 'Seismo', rustling up an illusory combo of artificial and live sonics - properly RIYL early Squarepusher, Matmos or Mira Calix.

When roles are so clearly demarcated, it can be hard to keep things challenging. Magaletti's a percussionist first and foremost, while Torsing is clearly happiest working on the DAW or behind the decks, but neither artist wanted their collaboration to be quite so predictable. So they figured out a way to make their respective roles  a little more complicated; after recording Magaletti's acoustic parts in Amsterdam's labyrinthine Rijksmuseum, Torsing decided to compliment them with digital percussion - mallet-style instruments that mimic or at least harmonize with Magaletti's elements. The result is a puzzling assembly of samples, sequences and breathless improvisations that injects some much-needed energy into the '90s Artificial Intelligence scaffolding Torsing has been respraying for the last few years.

Opener 'It comes to an end' yanks us back to Squarepusher's beardy jazz crossover era, or Matmos's ace early electroacoustic experiments. But Torsing and Magaletti keep things fresh, offsetting their ornate biomechanical flurries with Reich-ian minimalist phrases and xenharmonic prangs that keep us on our toes. It's unashamedly percussive material and yet plays like a sequence of lullabies, its virtuosic drumwork (just check the smoove editing on 'Superimposed') almost inevitably offset by music box chimes or cloudy, dreamlike pads. The other element that sets the duo apart is the vocals; peppered throughout the album are dialog snippets that keep things confusing, countering their surreal twangs and iceberg-cracking whirrs with alien whispers that only just permeate the membrane.

Is there even a voice on 'Hyperlocalize', or is it just our imagination? We can't be quite sure. But the garbled syllables are more audible on 'Mementoes', sandwiched between soothing, rubbery lead synths and hallucinated xylophones. Needless to say, if you're into anything from Plaid to Midori Takada, this'll be worth a closer listen.

items.body:
Returning after a 13 year absence, Boards of Canada's vision of hell isn't exactly surprising, swapping out the magic hour guitars of 'The Campfire Headphase' and the tired Carpenter-isms of 'Tomorrow's Harvest' for jagged distortions, dialog snippets and uneasy religious symbolism.

It can't be easy for Mike Sandison and Marcus Eoin; as soon as they cracked the code with 'Music Has the Right to Children' in 1998, their home-brewed signature sound - tape-warped, reverb-soaked monosynths, stuttering dialog samples and thumping MPC-breaks - became a sort of meme, regurgitated by a wave of bedroom musicians so frequently that the original references became fully hollow. Those early records were great because they sounded so unique, marking a landscape littered with post-'Chiastic Slide' crunches and choppy AFX-ian amens with new channels of thought. Just go back to their shadowy 'Twoism', 'Hi Scores', or that Mask 500 cover of 'Midas Touch' -  there was nowt else like it. By the time we got to 'The Campfire Headphase', a comparatively sunny, guitar-led misstep that arrived a few years later and then 2013's 'Tomorrow's Harvest' -  it all felt like diminishing returns.

'Inferno''s mysterious VHS rollout also felt overly familiar - and if you're gonna tease, the payoff best be worth it. Sadly, first single 'Prophecy At 1420 MHz' was damp and old fashioned, lumpen with boxy '80s drums and awkward prog rock synths - the signs didn't look good. Heard as a whole though, 'Inferno' hangs together pretty well. The brothers do a good job of laying out a vision of hell that's intricately connected to their well-worn source material: the lost future that was promised to wide-eyed 1970s kids raised on color TV, welfare and action figures. Back then, religious cults and street cranks were screaming of damnation, convincing weakened minds that judgement was coming while the Vietnam War raged - real hell was on the doorstep all along. And it's hard not to hear Boards' blend of seemingly old-fashioned religious symbolism (the Hare Krishna chants, chopped-up divinity school lectures and guided meditations) as an indirect reference to the wars raging right now. Certainly, it's their darkest album in years; not the aesthetic darkness of 'Tomorrow's Harvest', either. 'Father and Son', with its eerie Abrahamic symbolism, feels like an American Gothic reflection of Leslie Nielsen's comparatively benign narrations on 'Geogaddi', while 'Memory Death' feels like Boards actively sending off their own patented brand of hauntology with the EKG blip to prove it.

Throughout the record, BoC appear to juxtapose a cultural concept of hell with their own aesthetic responses, balancing dystopian robot voices with squelchy acid gurgles on the excellent 'The Word Becomes Flesh' and Bobby Beausoleil-style chiming strings on 'Blood in the Labyrinth'.  'The Process', meanwhile, offers a late-stage vision of aviation hell, a 'Langoliers'-style horror cue that neatly precedes the saccharine vintage BoC hit of 'You Retreat in Time and Space'. Perhaps unsurprisingly, it's these beatless moments that really hold things together - maybe they should have just leaned into it and done a full length of those vignettes. Still, 'Inferno' has its moments.

items.body:
Reissued almost 30 years after it arrived at Drag City HQ, U.S. Maple's third album was produced by Michael Gira and sharpens their noisy, Beefheart-inspired deconstructions, forming a nail-biting atmosphere of microtonal clangs, half-sung vocals and aborted rhythms that's still way, way out on its own.

U.S. Maple might get lumped in with Don Caballero and Shellac, but the further removed we are from peak math rock era, the more different they hit. In fact, listening back to 'Talker' now, it sounds more in line with gear from peers like Brainiac, Royal Trux and Gastr del Sol - it's hardly surprising to us that it was Jim O'Rourke who recommended them to Drag City back in 1999. And it was a prescient signing; they only released three more records but became one of the Chicago label's most defining acts. 'Talker' was a mark in the sand, a break from their Skin Graft era that showed a darker side to their sound: noisier, heavier, bleaker material that seemed to balance on Al Johnson's pained delivery and Mark Shippy and Todd Rittman's intertwined, dissonant riffs. For his part, drummer Pat Samson (who would leave the band just a couple of years after 'Talker' was tracked) seems to control the chaos, leaving fragments of rhythms in its dark corners, rather than laying down any kind of driving forward motion.

Musically, 'Talker' follows few of the math rock scene's core aesthetics. Johnson owes more to Pere Ubu's David Thomas, while the rest of the band seem to be deconstructing post-punk and no-wave standards in the same way that 'Trout Mask Replica' dispersed blues and country. There's even a waft of Keiji Haino's cracked noise/psychedelia when Johnson bellows over his bandmates' tempestuous roar of tangled strings and thudding, fractured rhythms. Hilariously, U.S. Maple toured with Pavement when 'Talker' was released, opening to boos from the crowds of frat slackers. Thankfully, the experience led them to dub the intricately divisive 'Acre Thrills', which might be even stronger. Crucial listening.

items.body:
Sydney-based drummer Laurence Pike lands on Balmat with a solo fusion of jazz, post-rock and trip-hop that nestles between Burnt Friedman, Makaya McCraven and Barry Adamson.

Remember Pivot? Or Triosk? The Leaf-signed experimental jazz outfit that famously fabricated the ace '1+3+1' LP with Jan Jelinek way back in 2003? Pike's been active on the international scene for what seems like forever - he even joined Liars in 2018. And 'Possible Utpias...' is his follow-up to 2024's ambitious "requiem mass for drums, electronics and choir" 'The Undreamt-of Centre'. Thankfully, this one's a little more approachable than that; there's no quartet to be found, it's just Pike and his gear, imagining what kind of music a jazz musician from an "idealized culture of the future" might make. 

It's a fascinating concept that drives a selection of impeccably played and produced sketches that Pike fleshes out with a little help from his friends: Ben Lerner on alto horn and Novak Manojlovic on keys. But it's Pike's affair and he's most successful when he disregards jazz altogether. On the excellent 'Night Bird', a whirring beat is juxtaposed with Michael Mann-like FM synths and an eerie, wide-open environment and the title track relegates Pike's percussion to the deep background, letting it scrape and scratch beneath dreamy electric piano repetitions.

Justin K. Broadrick aka Godflesh & Mick Harris aka Scorn - both one time members of Napalm Death - shell out the nastiest Brum techno clodhoppers on US label Give/Take.

Reprising a double team formation last heard on a split 12” in 2021, the elder statesmen of Birmingham techno and industrial musick deliver eight heavy duty cuts of bin bag-kicking club music. JK Flesh takes the lead with a batch of Regis-esque Brum techno, getting into a kinky, dubbed swing with ‘Conditional’ and slathering on the noise with ‘Transactional,’ beside the fang-toothed attack of ‘Disagreeable’ and Chi-spurred canter of ‘Used / User’ like a DJ Rush with a proper devilish glint in eye.

On the flip his former spar Mick Harris also throws back to the heyday of House of God and early Downwards with a rough batch of bangers taking in the overdriven romp ‘Night Before Rake’, cavernous warehouse shudder of ‘Slightly Over;’ and extra spicy shuffle of ‘Double Red’, plus the Surgeon-esque rave riff riddled into ‘Shelf.’

items.body:
STROOM fills in a gap on the timeline, excavating vital experiments made in Cologne in the wake of the cult 'Novaya Scena' compilation by Svitlana Nianio, Michael Springer, Guido Erfen, Soloveyka, Yewgeny Taran and Wolfram Burgtorf.

Back in 1993, a bizarre 20-track compilation appeared from Cologne's musical fringe. The idea for the set had come from artist and producer Erfen and sound engineer and percussionist Springer, two close friends who, taking advantage of cheap rent and disused buildings, put on regular events and established a recording studio in their neighborhood, off the beaten track. Erfen was a dedicated tape trader and had received a transmission from Kharkiv's Novaya Scena rock club that arrived with an essay and music from three local bands. At this time, Ukraine was still under Soviet rule and the music fascinated the two friends, shining a spotlight on a part of the world they were completely unfamiliar with. When singer and keyboardist Soloveyka visited cologne a year later, she handed Erfan more tantalizing music, inspiring him to make his own pilgrimage to Ukraine to investigate further. The research resulted in the 'Novaya Scene' CD, a set of tracks recorded between 1986 and 1992 that muddled prog with new wave, punk, folk and avant-garde rock. It was released on Hamburg's What's So Funny About label and was supposed to have a sequel.

That's where 'Aftermath and Transitions' comes in. Following the release of 'Novaya Scena', Erfen and Springer set up a series of sessions at their studio, inviting some of the Ukrainian artists to record with them. It's this period that resulted in Svitlana Nianio's 'Transilvania Smile' soundtrack that was properly released for the first time on Muscat sublabel Shukai in 2023. Nianio had been a member of Cukor Bila Smerť (the band who'd provided the stylistic anchor for 'Novaya Scena') and took the opportunity to launch her solo career, with Springer working as engineer. And there was more material from those sessions that Springer held back: the compilation's first four tracks are collaborations between Nianio, Springer, Taran and Springer's good friend Burgtorf. Opener 'Fake' was almost finished when Nianio showed up at the studio with her Casio in tow, so Springer plugged her in and she ended up lavishing the beat with vocals in Ukrainian and oddball keyboard vamps. The other three tracks were a little more organic, improvised in the studio while the artists got familiar with one another - there's the decelerated reggae experiment 'ManySpace', the instrumental groover 'Quiet Place' and best of all 'Політ Світляки', a wiry percussive jam that's not aged a day.

Erfen joins in on the ace exotica-tinged 'Whispering Walls' and 'Tired River', tracks from the group's final session in 1995. Nianio and Taran were planning to renew their visas and return to Cologne to record more, but it never happened - the recordings were shelved and the artists went about their lives independently. Then there's the three Solar tracks recorded by Soloveyka and Burgtorf who struck up a friendship after meeting at Springer's studio. Singing in Russian and English, Soloveyka breathes cabaret energy over Burgtorf's jerky, sample-heavy ethno-groove productions. And it's left to Taran to finish things off, with a "1996 Version" of his 'Death and the Bachelor' track that features none other than Nianio on keys. Phew. It's a brilliant set, really - not just one for STROOM obsessives, it'll speak to anyone whose interest in the Ukrainian underground was piqued by 'Transilvania Smile' or Muscut's ace Cukor Bila Smerť anthology.

In 'The Rhythm of Design', Zurich-based fine arts duo Michael Meier & Christoph Franz explore urban displacement and its impact on the local music scene.

"Focusing on six venues that have disappeared or are under threat, the artists collected materials on site - wood, metal, and other architectural elements and, with the support of professional instrument builders, transformed them into six musical instruments. Six artists and groups connected to these spaces, namely Kalabrese, Tobibi Ferrari-Bienz, Rafal Skoczek, Lucien Badoux & Jeremy Sauter, Nicola Kazimir, and Dualism each composed a piece for them, forming the basis for site-specific performances in September 2025. Rather than performing as an ensemble, the works ranging from experimental funk and punk to kraut, noise, and drone unfolded simultaneously in spatial fragments at the original locations. Only through movement and listening across the city did the composition emerge as a whole. The work was realized in collaboration with the City of Zurich, Art in Public Space (KiöR). Eight months after the original performances took place, the pieces are released via Switzerland-based publishing platform Präsens Editionen."

Sandy B’s classic ‘90s SA kwaito templates are lent a subtly trippy, brooding sidespin by Belgian DJ, producer and compiler soFa Elsewhere, sealed with artwork by Cape Town’s Darren Christian.

‘Forward in Reverse (Pt. 1)’ is a crafty effort at replicating and adapting a sound perhaps best recognised for the likes of Sandy B’s ‘AmaJovi Jovi’ heater of ’94, as reissued to cult acclaim in 2017 by Awesome Tapes From Africa. One of only a handful of efforts at reviving the sound that we can recall, the seven tracks nail an ace balance of the OG ‘90s sound - a sort of ruggedly hypnotic, slower take on deep house - with more psychedelic detailing and added political impetus in Sandy’s pointed lyrics, which sometimes slip into english from his native KwaZulu-Natal region’s Zulu tongue. The difference can be attributed to Sandy B’s lived experience of the past 30 years since ‘AmaJovi…’ and the moodier tone of soFa Elsewhere’s input, perhaps emphasising a long latent parallel with ‘80s hip house or Belgian new beat’s pace and purpose. 

Sandy voices each cut in a mix of choral harmony, undulating sing-song and rapped spoken word, flowing effortlessly between them on opener ‘Mangamanga’, or suitably kitted with new beat-esque heave-ho and wickedly scribbly synth on ‘Siren Work’, and sunken to moodiest hunch on ‘Khuluma Kakhulu.’ His politics come to the fore in the exasperated delivery and refrain “what’s wrong with you / you selfish bastard” on the (corruption) house grind of ‘Politicians’ and taken to slowest, dankest levels in ‘Eat Promises’, or like a mardy Francis Bebey in ‘ Mo-fucka’, and the martial swag of ‘Isosha Elidakiwe (Drunk Soldier)’ could almost have emerged from the Teknokrat’s studio in ’89.

More gorgeous, hazed dreamweaving from mysterio label wherethetimegoes - the same crew that gave us a pair of stunners from Princ€ss and Nashpaints, here dissolving Dublin's special blend of peak Celtic futurism into a suite of effervescent fiddle-laced electroacoustic experiments that turn everyday musical elements into vivid, lysergic space-age landscapes, smeared with VHS infidelities.

Like Princ€ss, we've no idea who Dublin are - they're a "post modern classical" duo, as far as we can tell - but there's at least a breadcrumb trail. They emerged back in 2022 on wherethetimegoes with a CDr of bizarre jams, seemingly on violin and synth, that put them fully into their own zone, seamlessly blending Celtic folk music, West Coast new age, Eno-esque ambient and downtown-era improv without even trying to flex. 'Heavy Dublin' picks up where that set left off, presenting a similarly anonymous sequence of jams that pack into roughly the same creative space. "Oh," a voice exclaims in the opening seconds of 'Untitled 4', heralding a thick wall of digital synths and soundscapes that's sliced thru by a Conrad-esque pitch-wonked violin performance that's amplified in a way that's at odds with the other sounds. It's almost drawing a line in the sand, exclaiming that the fiddle is from our world and doesn't need to be sculpted to fit into another. And it's the perfect introduction.

On 'Untitled 2', the vibrating, powdery fiddle improvisations shiver across the kind of rhythmic, metallophone-like synth loops that you might find on any number of early Detroit techno b-sides. It's a canny reference, using two distinct future projections to create something new, an off-world cogitation from an unmistakably contemporary source that projects past the stratosphere towards a 'Solaris'-style space station. And the atmosphere continues to grow on 'Untitled 3', with subtlly glitchy rhythmic interjections that interrupt the flow of brushed aluminum synths and mangled acoustic instrumentation. It's Visible Cloaks' Fairlight futures meets Laura Cannell's archeofiction, a muddle of imaginations that pull us backwards and forwards on the timeline all at once. Similarly, there's a trace of Arthur Russell's reverb-heavy 'World of Echo' steez on 'Untitled 7', caught in a tangle of bit-chewed samples and noisy digital outbursts.

The album seems to build up to 'Untitled 5', a weightless cloud of steel pan loops, obscured voices, chimes and harmonically rich fiddle scrapes that sounds as if it's hanging off the timeline by a thread, linking Takehisa Kosugi's 'Catch Wave' concept into a catalog of sounds that you'd more readily find in the world of tape traders and private press 12"s. Fully mind-melting gear, no doubt.

Including rare and long-lost tracks from Caustic Window (Aphex Twin), Tranquility Bass, Spacetime Continuum, and more, comes with a 20-page booklet packed with photos, artwork, and memorabilia from 1992–1995 and liner notes by founding members Mario Aguera and Kevin Foakes and an Obi strip featuring Simon Reynolds’ quote from Energy Flash

Hardcore jungle revival label Fundamental Frequencies gouch out with a gorgeous ode to pivotal chill out party Telepathic Fish, compiling blissed kisses from the likes of its regular DJ Mixmaster Morris, aka The Irresistible Force, and live performers AFX (Caustic Window), Global Communication and NoW, packaged with an illustrated, 20-page zine 

Who wants a head massage/back rub?! One for fluffier ravers and backroom posse; ‘Telepathic Fish: Trawling The Early 90s Ambient Underground’ yields a head-first dive into sublime waters that flowed around, between likemind labels such as Warp, Ninja Tune, and Rising High, and quenched crowds’ thirst for esoteric alternatives to full-bore rave. 

Originating in the sacred spaces of second rooms, squats and house parties, but soon enough a main room attraction in its own right, the Telepathic Fish events were run by Chantal Passamonte (aka Mira Calix - RIP), David Vallade, Mario Aguera and Kevin Foakes (aka DJ Food) - collectively named Openmind - who would be joined by the sound’s standard bearer Mixmaster Morris to throw a series of events in London often distinguished by their decor installations and paralleling similar happenings like Megatripolis, who were also informed by a certain sort of ‘60s-into-‘90s spirituality and techgnostic futurism.

Compiled by Mario, David and Kevin with fellow space cadet Chantal in mind, the picks and sequencing are impeccable and hold up the sound in its lushest light. The Irresistible Force’s remix of Barbarella is tumescent with loved-up glow, and NoW’s downbeat bliss-out ‘Nights Interlude’ is still adorable despite its ubiquity of that time. Global Communications’ ‘Incidental Harmony’ needs a Fish branded bean bag to cushion your swoon, and the nostalgia keeps on keeping on with RDJ’s deliciously whimsical ‘Cordialatron’, thru David Morley’s inversion of Golden Girls trance glyder, along with lesser known but no less loveable gems in No Man’s vignette or Keiichi Suzuki’s scalp-tingling ambient house trodder.

Posthumous reminder of MF Doom’s landmark classic, following the late, great MC’s death at the end of 2020 - with 11 tracks of bonus material.

A staple of our listening diet upon release in 2004 (probably preceded or followed by a listen to his ‘Special Blends volumes), ‘MM….Food’ still stands up among the greatest and most coveted hip hop albums of our time. Beats to bars, it’s a peerless example of Daniel Dumile Thompson’s MF Doom alias, playing out as a sort of stoned comic book fantasy voiced by a cartoon supervillain, literally inspired by Marvel Comics’ Doctor Doom, whose moniker sounds a bit like MF’s real middle name.  

The album oscillate between Doom’s mind-boggling metaphoric wordplay and his signature instrumentals, adapting the golden era ‘90s style of sampledelic collage and rugged rhymes to his singular purpose, and making a marked step on from his earlier work as Zev Love X with the legendary KMD. By choice or osmosis there’s probably a whole generation of headz who’ve committed the bars of ‘MM….Food’ to memory, and we can only recommend a refresher session right here if you’re rusty. Packing bags of nostalgia and vibes for days, it’s a true evergreen.

items.body:
One of thee heaviest records of the C.21st - stoner rock or otherwise - returns to orbit with a 20 year reissue of Al Cisneros & Chris Hakius frankly fucking sexy Om debut - essential FFO Sleep, Earth, Sunn 0))), Les Rallizes Dénudés, Father Dionysis Tabakis.

Like the ultimate death fart of twentieth century rock, ‘Variations on a Theme’ utterly reeks of leather, ganja, incense and stale booz, and that only makes us love it so much more. On three keeling parts Al Cisneros’ flaming riffs and monotone vox knit with Chris Hakius’ slow swingeing stickwork in longform mantras that have stuck in mind since its day of release, and have long become a go-to when nothing else will suffice. That may sound like blasphemy to disciples of Cisneros & Hakius’ former incarnation as ‘90s stoner rock/doom metal pioneers Sleep - infamous for inclusion on the Gummo soundtrack - but we’ll take Om over them any day. A hill we’ll die on, with this album blasting full volume.

Like the hellbound offspring of Led Zeppelin, Black Sabbath, and Popol Vuh, the duo set extraordinary levels in the A-side ‘On the Mountain at Dawn’, channelling heavy histories of modal hard rock and aspects of Tibetan, Byzantine, and Ethiopian mysticism into 23 minutes of molten churn that does not let go. It just builds and collapses into itself with a peerless, sustained intensity of vision, making the slightest changes feel like epic moments, and saving a turbo-charged afterburn for the 2nd half, when the driving cymbals double up and the riff goes full sicko mode. Throw in the B-side’s slower, slightly more succinct heck of ‘Kapila’s Theme’ and reaper-scythed percussion that pushes the axe to new depths on ‘Annapurna’, and you have a total masterpiece that hits like nowt else.

items.body:
Forever Records presents an extensive reissue edition of the first 'fully released' Psychick Warriors Ov Gaia album.

"Dancing on the wildest edge of the 90s outsider techno zeitgeist while proudly independent of any so-called scene, Ov Biospheres And Sacred Grooves: A Document Ov New Edge Folk Classics is both of its time and out of time. Rooted in the experiments of electronic music pioneers, industrial culture and ethnic music from around the globe while responding to the house and techno explosion, Robbert Heynen, Reinier Brekelmans, Reinoud van den Broek and Tim Freeman's freewheeling masterpiece takes in lush electronica and murky abstraction on its singular voyage through parts unknown.

Originally released in 1992, this is the first time the full, previously CD-only, version of Ov Biospheres and Sacred Grooves will be pressed on vinyl. The original LP and CD artwork from the various editions released in the early 90s has been combined and designed by the band, and the audio has been remastered with their full approval. 

Forever Records is a reissue series dedicated to rediscovering lost musical treasures from across the spectrum of head-feeding, heart-rending electronic music. Established by Rush Hour co-founder Christiaan Macdonald and Delsin founder Marsel van der Wielen, Forever Records places heartfelt faith in a carefully curated sequence of seminal, largely forgotten records from disparate eras, scenes and spaces within electronic music history. Tipped towards the mellow and introspective, these are albums that stop time when the needle hits the groove, stirring only when it's time to flip over before you sink back into the experience. That's what albums were always meant to be about, back then, right now, always and forever."

Mesmerising, illuminated sound environments conjured by Werner Durand, a key foil of CC Hennix & Amelia Cuni, joined by his Cuni spar Uli Hohmann on Mid-Eastern drums, Tibetan bells, and electronics on three intrepid, rhythmic drone excursions calling to mind Michael Ranta, Robert Rutman, Jon Hassell.

"WERNER DURAND has made himself a name with various projects with Dhrupad singerAMELIA CUNI, playing with URBAN SAX, ARNOLD DREYBLATT, HENNING CHRISTIANSEN, DAVID BEHRMAN, ELLEN FULLMAN, CATHERINE CHRISTER HENNIX, as the co-founder of THE 13th TRIBE, ARMCHAIR TRAVELLER and TONALIENS (with ROBIN HAYWARD and HILARY JEFFERY) plus numerous solo albums, released on labels like Black Truffle, Unseen Worlds or Edition Telemark. Having studied saxophone as well as Indian / Persian flutes, the Berlin based DURAND is a highly reputated protagonist in the drone scene, famous for his self-built wind instruments like buzz-clarinets or his PVC neys & horns.

His partner in FLOCKS (and longtime personal friend) is ULI HOHMANN whose early encounters with music from Asia, India and Africa led to studies with the Ghanaian master drummer MUSTAPHA TETTEY ADDY and later Tombak and Daf with NEMAD DARMAN (Iran). HOHMANN played in a couple of projects that explored the language of classical Persian music, and started building his own stringed instruments (being an educated carpenter). In 2014 he joined DURAND and AMELIA CUNI for the album "Clearing", and 2018 DURAND and HOHMANN decided to continue as a duo: FLOCKS was born.

On "Lagoon", the duo further explores the aesthetics it has crafted on its selftitled debut (2023, on the now defunct ZEHRA imprint): DURAND and HOHMANN shape drone-y soundscapes based on their self-built wind- & stringed instruments, Persian percussion and subtle electronics, drawing additional inspiration from Krautrock (listen to the irresistible, hypnotique, ever-changing rhythmic pattern of the title track) as well as JON HASSELL's "fourth world" aesthetics, placing the duo nicely between tradition and experiment!"

The roots of so much modern groove-driven music are reflected in Soundway’s study of rare jazz, calypso and drum music from ‘70s Trinidad & Tobago, the Caribbean nation off the coast of Venezuela.

In that time between artists first plugging in their instruments, and computerising them, the psychedelic sheen and sonification of US & UK pop and dance musics would also rub off on modernisers in the Caribbean. Under the Trinidadian term for calypso, “kaiso” the artists showcased here would blend Afro-American and West Indian traditions with certain studio innovations from disco and psych-rock to a clear purpose: driving dances - and everything that comes with them - in their lush isles.

The results are hip-gripping, heat-seeking gems that factor Black Atlantic links for a new, independent era un-tethered from colonial influence, ranging from the deeply soul-stirring jazz hush and rumble of ‘Ogun’ by Clive Zanda, thru Abdul Malik de Coteau’s plangent lament set to air-rippling steel drums, taking in the spiritual Latin jazz of Michael Boothman’s ‘Tabu’ brimming with optimism, to the muy caliente calypso of Andre Tanker, heads-down drum vibrations of Mansa Musa, and psych-funk fusioneering of Frends on ‘Mystery Music’.

items.body:
Following records on Quiet Time and Miami's Schematic, Cairo-based producer Mostafa Onsy arrives on the mighty Drowned By Locals with a unique adaptation of 808 Mafia's iconic trap sound that pulls in influences from classic '90s Egyptian pop and mahraganat.

'Baba Fen' might come as a surprise if you've heard Onsy's previous records, like 2021's dark, trippy IDM suite 'MetaConc' and its predecessor, a nostalgia trip that took its blueprint from AFX's '90s gear. Here, the producer takes his cues from Southside, TM88 and Lex Luger's iconic Atlanta trap productions: the ratcheting hi-hats, overdriven 808 kicks and acidic trance risers that characterized American music in the wake of breakouts from Future. Honestly, it works - we've long maintained the similarities between IDM's skittering beats and trap's, and Onsy's a natural, dropping a familiar ATL snare and FL Studio synths between mahraganat hand drums and those ubiquitous pitched hi-hat runs on the scene-setting 'Zabet Ekaa3 (Intro)'.

He's joined by local vocalists Fara7 and Bleng on 'Fnan', who help assert the album's Egyptian relevance, draping their melancholy AutoTuned slurs and ad-libs around Onsy's clever fusion of half-speed local percussion and trap's signature soundset. And the two MCs are joined by gravelly-voiced rapper Sakt on the album's brilliant title track, where Onsy supplies his spookies FM-laced beats, phonk-adjacent slaps that wouldn't be out of place on one of Raider Klan's early mixtapes. Rubber-voiced Drowned By Locals regular illfeel shows up on 'Fantanyel' and goes toe-to-toe with Bleng on 'Blikii', trading blows over one of Onsy's most ominous productions. Recommended.

Polish performance artist, musician, and poet Wojciech Kosma spills the contents of his heart on 'Tajemnica', a postmodern pop deconstruction that's between David Sylvian and Yung Lean.

There's a confusing quality to 'Tajemnica' that makes it difficult to engage with at first. It's produced almost ineptly, made with demo-like sounds that create a haze of preset nostalgia around Kosma's voice. It's only after a few tracks that the sound rights itself, and Kosma's intention makes itself clear. The record couldn't be any other way; the minimalism of the production just makes his voice stand out even more. Listen to the ominous 'Skrzydła', where a beat barely scratches the surface of Kosma's light synths - it's left to his lyrics, in Polish of course, to do the heavy lifting. And when different club sounds are referenced, it's inevitably oblique - a dancehall beat here, a log drum there. The sketchiness makes it sound like pop music that's been plucked out of a brain scanner, not completely whole, but not inhuman either.

This is pure class! Bobby Ingham’s darkly cinematic debut LP seriously strikes a nerve for admirers of Space Afrika, Mark Leckey, Burial & Low End Activist with its evocation of life in C.21st West Yorkshire manifest in a tensely paranoid, homesick patch-work of knifed samples wrapped up in weightless grime & UKG structures

‘Angel Of The North’ inarguably hits a high water mark of Sneaker Social Club’s retro-futurist UK fixations with a deeply impressive demonstration of sound design tekkerz at the service of immersive, narrative-driven impressionism. For 30 mins the 24 year old Ingham belies his yung years with a grasp of melancholic pathos, atmospheric subtlety and articulate crud that one may expect from an artist years his senior. He effectively has us rapt front to back, from the frisson of noctilucent pads and dread subs in ‘Lynne’ to the lush resolution of ‘I Can’t Believe It’, hustling listeners heavy into what the label term a “social-realist inversion of sound system music that relishes negative space while telling a street-level story.”

That story is most suggestively limned via judicious sampling from a mix of personal and public archives, diffused across a spectra of ghostly, ephemeral arrangements perfused with flashes of the music he grew up with; from snatches of Wonder & T2 in the chamber grime abstract ‘Easy Mush’, thru skipping UKG reduced to Burial-esque degrees on ‘WYD Tomorrow Night.’ But it’s the poetic sense of restraint and sensuality that practically makes it a spiritual successor to label boss Low End Activist’s own evocation of life growing up on Oxford council estates (‘Hostile Utopia’ & ‘Municipal Dreams’), and clearly comparable to Mark Leckey’s collaged art-film soundtracks as much as the northern romanticism of Space Afrika’s liminal ambiance, or even EXLRUTH’s chamber adaptations of makina in its dare-to-differ approach and spellbinding effect. 

Big tip!

A Detroit house/jazz masterpiece, 2004, mercifully back in circulation on vinyl for as long as stocks last (ie, not long) - don’t think twice if you spent the last 20 years kicking yourself for missing out - really is the GOAT.

'Black Mahogani’ first landed some 10 years into Kenny Dixon Jr.’s catalogue and firmly pinned him on the map with its hugely ambitious scope and attention to detail. His 5th and arguably most celebrated studio album, it’s also by far his most coveted, partly due to being neglected from reissue schemes, which has led to a status that’s grown in step with KDJ’s renown. 

It still fully kills with ten top shelf cuts sifted from prized 12”s dating back to the late ‘90s and here stitched with exclusive gear into a sort of deep jazz soundtrack updated with a Detroit house heartbeat and leagues-deep soul, effortlessly bridging epochs with timeless steez.

To pluck a few jewels from its crown, centrepiece ’Shades of Jae’ is a masterclass in deferred kick drum gratification that never fails in the dance, and the lush, jazz-taught sashay of ‘Runaway’ and sampledelia of ‘Mahogani 9000’ still take our breath away. But it’s really all best taken in longform context, from the first frisson of hi-hats and Roberta Sweed’s aching croon on ‘Holiday’ thru the filter chicanery of a closing title tune that only sets one up to do it over and again...

Aged well this one, Steven Hitchell aka Echospace aka Intrusion with set of analogue dubs very much in the spirit of Rhythm & Sound, including a strong contribution from Paul St. Hilaire aka Tikiman just to complete the act of worship. Now 15 years since it was last in circulation, the album has been remastered and is available as a double LP for the first time ever.

The Deepchord/Echospace axis is definitely having a moment. After a period where it was dismissed by some as a sort of unnecessary facsimile of Mark & Moritz’s OG blueprint, the benefit of hindsight has marked Hitchell and Modell’s productions as very much their own thing, still indebted to Berlin, but with their own signature. 

Perhaps it’s the analogue production that lends the material an air of slightly uncontrolled brilliance; the hiss of the mixing desk feels tangible rather than just digital decoration - less cosplay, more weighty and propulsive.

However - be in no doubt - if you’ve a love for anything on the line from Basic Channel to M-Series, Main Street, Burial Mix, Rhythm & Sound and Chain Reaction, this stuff is absolutely your next port of call - and this one here is one of the best from the label too, just check the clips and you’ll know exactly where you are.

Known to 313 locals for his colourful murals all over the city, and on this sleeve, Sheefy McFly also trades in a mean vein of uptempo booty music, as heard at his Ghettotechtopia parties and recently on a self-released LP and an ode to local ghetto-tech hotspot, ‘Belle Isle 2099’. His ‘Baddies Only’ EP elevates a signature sound of scudding 808 bass, claps, and keys with a spotlight on six original vocalists from his ends, each characteristic of classic-contemporary Motor City club music and its bridges to Chicago ghettotech.

From the front, he loops bars by duo Etherpussy on undulating subs and electrosoul chords in a style shared by Lola Damone’s bars on ‘Pretty World’, and also calling to mind Andrés’ class GT Flips - a reference point for the choppier soul of ‘You’re Mine’, which tilts more into footwork angularity. Tiptonaires also brings a fierce but warm energy with her faux naïf bars on the chromatic synths of ‘Cute2Nite’, while your trunk’s Cerwin Vegas get a proper test in the Miami Bass-type tremors of ‘Young N Turnt’, voiced by DJ Mobetta.

Party guaranteed!

items.body:
Recorded straight to tape in Glasgow, poet/performer Lisa Jones and VOM's Chas Lalli's Gilchard debut is refreshingly human, a grotesque blend of ugly reality and absurdity that situates itself between Electrelane, Arab Strap, Dry Cleaning and early Factory biz.

'Chins for Lefty' might be Gilchard's first recording, but Jones and Lalli are hardly newcomers. Since the mid-'00s, Lalli has been a member of Glaswegian post-punk/noise rock trio VOM, moonlighting in Bad Aura and the art-punk outfit Dragged Up, where he first collided with Jones. A writer and poet with a background in the local spoken word/improv scene, Jones' lyrics provide the backbone for Gilchard's sound, building a surreal parallel Glasgow that Lalli meets head-on with jangling guitars, frazzled drum loops and murky synths. Even the recording process itself plays a part, lending the album a timeless quality - honestly if you assured us this was an excavated private press gem from the late '80s we'd probably believe you.

"I turn your picture to face the wall," Jones deadpans on 'Posthumous Hologram', breaking her monotone to sing a real chorus while Lalli stacks organ vamps and Vini Reilly guitars in the space beneath. And the duo decelerate their sound significantly on 'Break Up with Johnny Dogbirth', sounding as heroin-addled as The Velvet Underground as they work in slow motion, batting emotional reflections to each other over an almost inaudible drum beat.

After slaying with her cold fusions of ’90s R&B, ’00s brukfunk and footwork on 2024’s ‘Concentrate’ EP and last year’s ‘Come Alive’ album, NZO returns with a deadly hyper-jiggy session for DDS - huge one FFO Various Production, Beatrice Dillon, Dolo Percussion, Rian Treanor, Akufen, El-B.

Captured at Rotherham Minster (the finest perpendicular church in Yorkshire, don’t u know) for SoYo’s annual electronics music showdown, No Bounds, NZO’s custom-built results brim with an unusual grasp of the funk, prompting a uniquely jittery rush offset with a wicked refusal of rhythmic anticipation that does crazy things with your limbs. With the finest grasp of ghost snares and the confidence to slap and tickle drums where others wouldn’t, she deftly dances thru fresh routes of rhythmic pursuit. Low-key, this sort of experimental ingenuity betrays her background in the sciences, as much as a keen ear for offbeat and upfront dance musics -  effortlessly joining and short-circuiting oblique dots between Timbaland x The Neptunes’ rugged nuance, El-B’s whipsmart torsion, RP Boo’s legwork and Beatrice Dillon’s precision-tooled arrangements, all gelled with daring confidence in her own thing. 

We can't tell you if NZO's a DJ or nah, but she approaches her set with a serious understanding of how to take control of your limbs, linking rhythms, samples and melodic phrases as if she's grandstanding on four CDJs. She rushes towards euphoria with truncated R&B coos that she expertly threads between dub stabs and garage-y organ vamps, keeping the jerky rhythms intact throughout. And just when you think you've tapped in, sugar-sweet vocals and brassy fanfares cut into a shudder of drums, an 'ANTI EP'-era AE bass whoosh comes out of nowhere to remind you where you are. 

NZO patches together an authentically Yorkshire-coded reaction to New York's post-GHE20G0TH1K evolution, the self-consciously p2p-driven movement that helped shape visionary DJs like Total Freedom and Juliana Huxtable. But she’s less conspicuously "deconstructed" than her predecessors and champions Sheffield's avant history, referencing Warp's early run, Mark Fell's continuous influence and the perpetual grind of heavy industry, blending these elements with her spectrum of influences from further afield. Freaky, hyper-articulated movers need to check it at the nearest opportunity, trust.

You can just drop the needle and close your eyes for a near 20 minutes of fathomless sonic depth, massaging your brain and mind, a deep dive into an immersive analogue world. A new addition to this newly minted vinyl iteration of the "Altering Illusions" series now includes cv313's blistering analogue assault on the darkest radius bit in the interpolation tapes series. Expect sub-harmonic deep space exploration in some seriously out-there electronic quadrants, some of the deepest techno reductions ever captured to tape!"

items.body:
Luke Slater’s pioneering bleep techno vessel PAS returns to a club landscape that he helped spawn in the ’90s, with a striking exposition of techno purism primed for the new wave of pouting pumpers.

Beamed in direct from his Space Station Ø studio for longtime patrons Ostgut Ton, ‘Planetary People’ trades in a patented style of machine music that Slater, along with Detroit legends such as Jeff Mills, Claude Young, and Terrence Dixon, plus European heads Donato Dozzy or Steve Bicknell, have made into the the prevailing sound of Berlin and contemporary techno clubs worldwide. 

Slater’s feel for effortless momentum continues to make his work stand out from the crowd on these 13 new missives, each eagerly awaiting application in warehouse endurance tests and late-for-work crosstown trots. As such it rolls out in thru-line for those who consume albums as intended, with expert harness and whip control from the acid afterburn of intro ‘Into the Night’ to what sounds like Konono No.1 at Berghain in ‘Labyrinth’, peak time canter in ‘Thunder Major’, and 9 minutes of sublime tension to closer ‘Presently My Soul Grew Stronger’.

But if you just need to big rockets, ‘Quadrant 10’ will electrify any ‘floor with its rattling buzz, and the tight knit arps of ‘Brave Cosmo’ will piston tendons along with the cavernous slay of ‘Retina Burn’, and you just know the recoiling bounce of ‘Beton Brut’ is going to soundtrack some of the heaviest club and festival moments of summer ’26 and beyond.

items.body:
Bruce remixes Quade's 2025 LP 'The Foel Tower' on a limited cassette for his Poorly Knit label.

"Back in 2023, Bruce was approached by a band of young and ambitious lads, who wanted him to mix their debut album 'Nacre'. Being fans of his music, they hoped to utilise his renowned, club-informed and emotive sound design to add a shade of hypnotism and psychedelia to their singular strand of post-rock. The band of course were Quade, and the union proved to make perfect sense: Bruce excelled in gracefully fulfilling the band's vision, sealing their relationship for projects to come.

A couple years on, both Quade and Bruce had really proved the scope of their abilities: the sophomore album 'The Foel Tower' won the hearts of fans and critics across the board, who celebrated its "gorgeous" and "tender" sound to great acclaim. The world they had built clearly stood defined and dignified, though at the same time, Bruce couldn't help but wonder if there was more to be said. Besides, the sheer abundance of emotion and rich textures therein, suggested a great deal of potential for further exploring. So with the band’s blessing, he embarked on versioning the album.

Bruce was off the leash: total freedom leant him the ability to dub in wild style, weaving and wrestling with drum, bass et al, connecting to the arrangements' true feelings and expanding them to full frame. The "doomer sad boy, ambient-dub, folk, experimental post-rock" of the original, was blown into a whole new, hypnotic realm: through rattling analogue distortion and huge spaced out effects, Bruce's efforts stand as an exploding supernova of dub and noise, refracted through the band's themes of grief, beauty and the great British countryside.

To be released on his label Poorly Knit, this remix album once again proves Bruce's deft of touch and skill in reworking material. Maximising the sonic potential of such a promising and talented band he marks his personal contribution towards what will surely continue to be a fulfilling and illustrious musical journey for Quade."

A seminal, early highlight of shoegaze that helped birth the idea of “dream pop”, also serving as a blueprint of sorts for Dean Blunt's world of sound, A.R. Kane’s debut album is among the most under-sung, yet foundational, records of its time. 

A.R. Kane were no doubt an anomaly in their field - far as we know, the only Black band of musicians operating in British indie-pop-rock music - which only makes their dare-to-be-different style even more exceptional, in hindsight. They would famously go on to create a major touchstone of acid house and dance-pop with their über-classic ‘Pump Up The Volume’ as M/A/R/R/S, but before that they released debut album ’SIxty Nine’, laying out a template for psychedelic, grooving pop music that remains practically peerless in its field, with echoes of its sound heard everywhere from Micachu & The Shapes to Dean Blunt in the current day. 

After 32 years ’Sixty Nine’ remains a most beautiful sore thumbs-up, with tenderly fragile yet powerful vocals set to a mix of psychedelia, dub, jazz-funk, free jazz spirits and keeling amounts of guitar feedback, in a style that the band’s Alex Ayuli would describe as “dream-pop” - a term which has stuck and blossomed ever since. Mercifully, “dream-pop” provides a catchy phrase for their hard-to-place sound for clumsy writers like we, and is practically the only way to encompass their sound here; taking in the range of their jangling sorta Afrobeat/indie hybrid styles in ‘Crazy Blue’, thru to swooning dub-rock-pop of ‘Baby Milk Snatcher’, the charred guitar feedback scapes of ’Sulliday’, and the thizz of their spine-tracing vox, guitar, and hi-hats in ‘Spermwhale Trip’, alongside the chamber-like oddity of ‘The Madonna Is With Child.’ And considering that it was issued in a pivotal year for new music, it’s always worth listening to Simon Reynolds’ take, who sums up ’69’ very neatly in his review for Melody Maker as “the outstanding record of ’88.”

Seriously there’s nowt quite like this album. A 100% must check if you don’t already know.

items.body:
Following last year's long-overdue reissue of 'bloweyelashwish', Numero deepen the narrative with a new edition of Lovesliescrushing's prescient second album 'xuvetyn', compiled from hissy cassettes 4-tracked between 1991-'95 and a crucial stepping stone between shoegaze, tape music and power ambient -  essential biz if you're anywhere on the line from MBV to Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, Flying Saucer Attack to Windy & Carl.

We're still not sure how this one passed so many people by when it appeared first time around, way back in 1996. 'xuvetyn' is the duo's most perfect statement, a record that lacks the sheer shock of their debut but surpasses it elsewhere on almost every level. Producer Scott Cortez and vocalist Melissa Arpin-Duimstra assembled the album over a five year period, slowly collecting rudimentary experiments with a few pedals and a busted TASCAM Portastudio. And unlike its predecessor, it sounds as if it's been rounded out at the edges - still noisy, of course, characterised by tape fuzz and distortion that positions them somewhere between 'Loveless' and 'Endless Summer', but it flows seamlessly, foreshadowing the next few decades of euphoric, shoegaze-adjacent ambient gear. 

Without exaggeration, Lovesliescrushing just puzzled out a sweetspot between noise, minimalism, euphoria and repetition a little earlier than the rest. Inspired by Robert Fripp, Cocteau Twins, Eno, Jon Hassell, Glenn Branca and, of course, MBV, you can hear exactly how they absorbed all those influences, stretching Arpin-Duimstra's breathy vocal next to swelling, almost orchestral guitar drones. Stars of the Lid would get the flowers for their own response to many of the same influences a few years later, and - by the mid '00s - a more organic, shoegaze-aware brand of "ambient" began to seep into the underground's top levels: Fennesz, Tim Hecker, Jefre Cantu-Ledesma and others. The crazy thing is, so many of those artists' ideas were prototyped here; using 4-track tape tricks rather than granular effects or Max/MSP patches - Cortez and Arpin-Duimstra inadvertently mapped out a language that would define the laptop age. Just listen to the FM gamelan-cum-bleep techno experiment 'Virgin Blue-Eyed' and tell us they weren't years ahead of their time.

Prophetic, essential gear.

items.body:
Jack Cooper and Tara Cunningham (1/2 of Modern Nature) present an LP as duo 'The Sleeves'.

"The Sleeves are the duo of Jack Cooper and Tara Cunningham, both likely known to you as one half of Modern Nature. Following an all-instrumental Mossy Tapes release last November, Cooper and Cunningham have recorded 10 new songs showcasing their vocal and guitar interplay with only the faintest echoes of prior efforts (individually or collectively), representing a fully realized leap forward from their largely improvised debut.

'The Sleeves' is a somewhat counter intuitive take on the guitar/vocal duo formula (provided you think there is such a thing) though it's not nearly as simplistic as "the space between the notes" - it would be the height of exaggeration to say an album this simultaneously expansive and incandescent is unprecedented. But it doesn't happen nearly often enough, either.

“What I initially found so familiar and exciting about playing guitar with Jack - and continually do - is that our approach to music is pretty much exactly the same. And that is - to celebrate the space that frames ideas, embraces silence, to play simply, simultaneously championing our respective unembellished guitar sounds, whilst looking for sounds that aren’t like a guitar at all - bells, birds, switching between radio stations etc. It’s rare to find someone who - whatever this means to you - ‘gets it’ - and I think when we started playing guitar together, we both knew the other had something of whatever our ‘it’ was.”

“‘The Sleeves’ is the sum of our shared musical journey thus far, an exciting mix of familiarity and uncharted territory in its approach to structure and how we use our guitars and voices. It feels to me like we are both citing shared references and traditions, whilst floating in our own, single-cell world that is completely genre-less. That grey area is where we seem to thrive. As Jack says, it feels like music that really couldn’t be made by anyone else.” - Tara Cunningham

“Tara and I started playing guitar together at the start of 2024. It was an improvised music night in a railway arch in South London. The set was great but there was a couple of minutes in particular where Tara and I really sort of locked in. We made a record a few weeks later. There was something in the way we played together that felt very intuitive from the start. We recognised a shared approach right away and an affinity to the way each other played.”

“During the summer we got stuck in a traffic jam coming home from a show in Glasgow. We spent a few hours singing along to the Mamas & The Papas and Simon & Garfunkel and over the course of the day, like magic we became The Sleeves. We're excited about it because it feels like music that really couldn’t be made by anyone else. We don’t bring different elements to it. We both bring exactly the same things. It’s the result of our similarities.” - Jack Cooper "

Following frontman Elias Rønnenfelt's indie throwback smash 'Speak Daggers', cult Danish band Iceage continue to shave down post-punk until it looks more like Britpop. RIYL Fontaines DC, Liars or Gilla Band.

It wouldn't be fair to say that Iceage divided its fanbase when they released the sleek 'Seek Shelter' back in 2021. The album was a surprise to their early champions who'd watched them move from noisy hardcore towards a Talking Heads-indebted post-punk sound, but it was also pretty universally acclaimed, its relative polish deemed acceptable because the songs were genuinely pretty catchy. 'For the Love of Grace & the Hereafter' arrives five years later and in the wake of Rønnenfelt's newfound notoriety - both as a solo star and a tabloid staple. So you can almost predict what direction the band have gone in; their sixth album is their most digestible yet, making its predecessor sound almost rough around the edges in comparison.

Rønnenfelt, for his part, actually sounds refreshed, his voice falling between Shane McGowan's and Bobby Gilespie's and for our money handling the pitchy oddball routine a lot more convincingly than Geese's Cameron Winter. But still, it's better suited to angular material like the Byrne-esque 'Match Head Girl' than it is to melodramatic indie-pop gear like 'No Fear' or Strokes-ish material like 'Tender Blades'. The album will probably be huge, it's just chewy like that - they should take Dean Blunt on tour with them.
